title: National Council for Adoption v. Blinken (2021)
shortTitle: National Council for Adoption v. Blinken (2021)
summary: The State Department’s categorical soft-referral prohibitions added duties that the existing best-interests standard did not establish.

sections.Parties: The National Council for Adoption, whose members included adoption agencies and attorneys, challenged State Department website guidance concerning international adoptions.
sections.Material Facts: The Department issued several 2018 notices describing prohibited “soft referrals.” They barred certain communications or matching practices before a child’s eligibility determination or prospective parents’ completed home study, including holding a child’s file in ways that excluded other families. Violations could threaten accreditation. The Department argued that its guidance clarified regulations requiring adoption in children’s best interests and completion of specified checks before placement.
sections.Procedural History: The district court dismissed for lack of standing. The D.C. Circuit held that the Council had standing and reached the fully briefed merits at the parties’ request under its stated practice for a clear legal question likely to generate another appeal. The excerpt resolves whether the guidance required notice and comment; it does not reproduce the final mandate’s wording.
sections.Issue: Did the guidance merely interpret existing obligations, or did it adopt new legislative prohibitions requiring notice and comment?
sections.Holding: The court held that the guidance was a legislative rule requiring notice and comment because it made new law by categorically prohibiting two types of soft referral.
sections.Reasoning: The general best-interests standard did not compel or logically justify the categorical restrictions. Circumstances involving biological relatives close to completing a home study illustrated why a blanket prohibition might not follow from that context-sensitive standard. Existing law required home studies before placement, which did not necessarily prohibit earlier informal matching. The Department’s claimed intention to clarify existing law could not supply a missing legal derivation. Notice and comment would let affected parties identify consequences and exceptions before adoption. The notes emphasize that the relevance of categorical language here stems from the flexible underlying legal text, rather than a universal rule that interpretive guidance must always be tentative.

sources.label: LRS-november-1-165(2).pdf · printed pp. 657–660 · physical PDF pp. 82–85

topics.lrs-n-interpretive-rules: A context-sensitive best-interests regulation did not logically require categorical soft-referral prohibitions.
